info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 2.2: Deterministic Schema Validation, Linked Data, and Canonical Citation.

name.text: 01 Question: What "Deterministic" Means in Structural Philology

questiontext.text: In computational philology and text encoding, what defines a process as deterministic?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic validation evaluates XML documents against explicit, rule-governed schemas, transforming subjective text entry into mathematically verifiable and interoperable research data.

answer.text: Identical inputs evaluated by explicit, rule-governed algorithms always produce identical, mathematically verifiable results without probabilistic variance.

feedback.text: Correct. Deterministic systems operate without statistical approximation or generative ambiguity, guaranteeing repeatable validation.

answer.text: The process relies on human editorial consensus to interpret ambiguous textual readings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human consensus involves subjective interpretation rather than algorithmic determinism.

answer.text: The system predicts the most statistically probable XML tag based on a neural language model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Statistical prediction is probabilistic, which is the opposite of deterministic validation.

answer.text: The validation engine automatically corrects syntax errors without throwing compiler warnings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic validation evaluates compliance against rules; it does not silently rewrite user files.

name.text: 02 Question: The Grammar of XML: Understanding RELAX NG (RNG)

questiontext.text: Why has the Text Encoding Initiative standardized on RELAX NG (RNG) as its primary schema definition language?

generalfeedback.text: RELAX NG provides the mathematical tree grammar that defines permissible element hierarchies, sequences, and datatypes across TEI digital editions.

answer.text: It is based on tree automata and formal grammars, offering a clean syntax that supports rich datatypes and flexible element patterns.

feedback.text: Correct. RELAX NG avoids the rigid constraints and complex syntax of DTDs and XSD while supporting full namespaces and regular expression patterns.

answer.text: It is the only schema language supported by web browsers for direct HTML rendering.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web browsers render HTML/CSS and do not execute RELAX NG validation.

answer.text: It completely replaces the need for ISO Schematron business logic rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RELAX NG handles local tree grammars, but still requires Schematron for cross-element assertions.

answer.text: It compiles XML documents directly into binary executable code for triple stores.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RELAX NG is a schema grammar for validation, not a compiler for binary triple stores.

name.text: 03 Question: Validating Your Hand-Written Header in VS Code

questiontext.text: How does an XML document formally associate itself with an external RELAX NG schema in VS Code?

generalfeedback.text: VS Code links XML documents to schemas via `` instructions, providing real-time background validation and diagnostics.

answer.text: Via <?xml-model?> processing instructions placed at the top of the file specifying the schema URI and schema type.

feedback.text: Correct. VS Code reads the <?xml-model?> instruction to automatically fetch the schema and provide real-time background validation.

answer.text: By embedding the complete C++ source code of the parser directly into the root <TEI> element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parsers are external executable engines referenced via lightweight processing instructions.

answer.text: By naming the XML file with the extension .rng instead of .xml.

feedback.text: Incorrect. .rng is the extension for the schema file itself, not for XML instance documents.

answer.text: By declaring schema definitions within the HTML <head> tag of the web browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI documents are XML, not HTML, and validation occurs in editors or CLI tools via processing instructions.

name.text: 04 Question: Structural Rules and Element Hierarchy in RNG

questiontext.text: What happens during RELAX NG validation if an encoder places <supportDesc> directly inside <msDesc> without enclosing it in <physDesc> and <objectDesc>?

generalfeedback.text: RELAX NG strictly enforces element containment and sequencing, ensuring that complex manuscript metadata is predictable and machine-traversable.

answer.text: The parser immediately halts and raises a validation error because the mandatory parent container hierarchy has been violated.

feedback.text: Correct. RELAX NG strictly enforces parent-child containment; intermediate structural containers cannot be omitted.

answer.text: The parser silently creates the missing parent tags and saves the file automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validators evaluate conformance and report errors; they never alter source documents silently.

answer.text: The parser accepts the element provided its @material attribute is set to parchment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Valid attributes cannot bypass illegal element containment in tree grammars.

answer.text: The document is downgraded to HTML5 format but remains schema-valid.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML validation is binary and strict; it does not convert documents to HTML.

name.text: 05 Question: Data Typing, Enumerations, and Attribute Constraints

questiontext.text: Why does the TEI schema require dates in attributes like @when or @notBefore to conform to ISO 8601 datatypes (such as YYYY or YYYY-MM-DD)?

generalfeedback.text: Schemas enforce ISO datatypes and controlled attribute enumerations, ensuring that chronological, numerical, and categorical values remain machine-computable.

answer.text: To ensure chronological values are machine-computable for sorting, temporal filtering, and algorithmic analysis across databases.

feedback.text: Correct. Standardized ISO formats allow algorithms to process time deterministically, while prose nuances belong in element text.

answer.text: Because premodern manuscripts were always dated using the Gregorian calendar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Premodern dates were often indictions, regnal years, or Julian dates; ISO normalisation is a modern computational requirement.

answer.text: To reduce the file storage size of the XML document on local hard drives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ISO date format is required for semantic computability, not file compression.

answer.text: Because XML parsers crash if an attribute contains alphabetic characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Attributes can contain text strings unless constrained to specific XML Schema datatypes by the schema.

name.text: 06 Question: Beyond Grammar: The Necessity of Schematron Business Logic

questiontext.text: Which validation challenge exposes the fundamental architectural limitation of RELAX NG and necessitates ISO Schematron?

generalfeedback.text: ISO Schematron complements RELAX NG by executing XPath-driven business logic and cross-element assertions that grammar-based schemas cannot evaluate.

answer.text: Verifying cross-element referential integrity, such as ensuring an @hand attribute targets a declared @xml:id elsewhere in the tree.

feedback.text: Correct. RELAX NG evaluates local parent-child grammars, whereas Schematron uses XPath to enforce document-wide relational business logic.

answer.text: Checking whether opening XML tags have matching closing tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Basic tag matching is a well-formedness rule evaluated by standard XML parsers.

answer.text: Enforcing that attribute values are enclosed in quotation marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Quoted attributes are a syntactic requirement of well-formed XML.

answer.text: Validating that the root element is named <TEI>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Root element naming is handled directly by RELAX NG grammar patterns.

name.text: 07 Question: Writing Schematron Rules for Internal Cross-References

questiontext.text: How does a Schematron rule verify that every <msItem> in a manuscript description includes valid locus coordinates?

generalfeedback.text: Schematron uses XPath assertions to audit internal cross-references and enforce mandatory editorial rules across the entire TEI document.

answer.text: By defining a <rule context="tei:msItem"> containing an <assert test="tei:locus[@from and @to]"> XPath expression.

feedback.text: Correct. Schematron evaluates the XPath test against each context node, raising a custom error message if the condition fails.

answer.text: By converting the XML document into a SQL table and executing an INNER JOIN query.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron operates natively on XML trees using XPath assertions.

answer.text: By running a regular expression search across the plain text file for the word 'folio'.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regular expressions on raw text ignore XML tree hierarchy and attribute semantics.

answer.text: By invoking an external machine learning model to predict missing leaf numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron is a deterministic rule-based validator, not a predictive AI model.

name.text: 08 Question: Customizing the TEI: The ODD (One Document Does-It-All) Architecture

questiontext.text: What is the primary operational advantage of the TEI ODD (One Document Does-it-all) architecture?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI ODD architecture generates project-specific RELAX NG schemas, Schematron rules, and human-readable documentation from a single XML source of truth.

answer.text: It generates machine-actionable schemas (RNG/Schematron) and human-readable documentation simultaneously from a single XML source of truth.

feedback.text: Correct. Compiling schemas and guidelines from one ODD file ensures technical validation rules and editorial prose never drift apart.

answer.text: It allows XML documents to be rendered in web browsers without using CSS or JavaScript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ODD manages schema customization and documentation, not client-side browser rendering.

answer.text: It automatically translates Greek and Latin manuscripts into modern vernacular languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ODD defines structural metadata schemas, not linguistic machine translation.

answer.text: It compresses 500 TEI elements into a single proprietary binary file format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ODD produces standard open XML schemas (RNG, XSD, Schematron) and HTML documentation.

name.text: 09 Question: Case Study: The Bodleian msdesc.odd Consolidated Schema

questiontext.text: Why did the Bodleian Library develop the consolidated msdesc.odd schema for its manuscript catalogue?

generalfeedback.text: Institutional repositories like the Bodleian Library use customized ODD schemas to enforce mandatory cataloguing constraints across diverse historical collections.

answer.text: To enforce mandatory institutional cataloguing standards and Schematron constraints across diverse departmental collections via automated CI pipelines.

feedback.text: Correct. A shared ODD ensures that all cataloguers and external contributors adhere to identical metadata requirements before ingestion.

answer.text: To restrict public access to manuscript shelfmarks and high-resolution images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema is open-source on GitHub and designed to facilitate public discovery.

answer.text: To eliminate the need for XML validation by relying exclusively on unstructured text files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The project enforces strict automated XML validation on every pull request.

answer.text: To replace physical manuscript conservation with digital 3D models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. msdesc.odd models codicological description, not physical conservation or 3D scanning.

name.text: 10 Question: Case Study: Bibliotheca Laureshamensis and the ENRICH Schema

questiontext.text: How did the Bibliotheca Laureshamensis – digital project use the TEI ENRICH schema to digitally reunite the dispersed library of Lorsch Abbey?

generalfeedback.text: The Bibliotheca Laureshamensis virtually reunited 331 dispersed Carolingian manuscripts across 73 institutions by using the TEI ENRICH schema as an automated validation gate.

answer.text: By establishing an automated validation gate that required 73 holding institutions across 13 nations to submit XML conforming to a unified codicological schema.

feedback.text: Correct. Strict automated schema validation enabled the seamless integration of descriptions from dozens of decentralized repositories.

answer.text: By physically purchasing all 331 surviving manuscripts and returning them to Germany.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manuscripts remain in their 73 dispersed physical repositories; reunification is digital.

answer.text: By discarding historical provenance metadata in favour of modern shelfmarks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reconstructing the lost monastic library depended heavily on detailed provenance encoding.

answer.text: By converting all Latin manuscripts into modern German translations before cataloguing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The project encodes primary codicological descriptions of the original Latin codices.

name.text: 11 Question: The Limits of Document Isolation: Why XML Needs Linked Open Data

questiontext.text: Why is a valid TEI XML document containing plain-text place names (like <origPlace>Alexandria</origPlace>) considered an isolated data silo?

generalfeedback.text: Unlinked XML documents remain isolated textual silos; Linked Open Data connects local strings to global semantic authorities, enabling automated cross-institutional computation.

answer.text: To a computer, the text string is ambiguous characters without semantic coordinates, preventing automated disambiguation or cross-repository linking.

feedback.text: Correct. Text strings cannot disambiguate between different places named Alexandria or link to gazetteers without persistent URIs.

answer.text: XML parsers refuse to validate documents that contain proper nouns in element text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Plain text is fully valid in XML; the limitation is semantic interoperability, not syntactic validity.

answer.text: Plain text strings cannot be indexed by search engines or displayed on web pages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Plain text is easily indexed by basic keyword search, but lacks structured semantic relationships.

answer.text: The TEI schema strictly forbids the use of the <origPlace> element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <origPlace> is a standard TEI element; the enhancement comes from adding URI attributes.

name.text: 12 Question: The Resource Description Framework (RDF) and Semantic Triples

questiontext.text: What are the three fundamental components of an RDF semantic triple?

generalfeedback.text: RDF models information as Subject-Predicate-Object triples, weaving disparate manuscript descriptions into a globally queryable semantic knowledge graph.

answer.text: Subject (URI), Predicate (Ontology Property URI), and Object (URI or Literal Value).

feedback.text: Correct. RDF models all knowledge as directed graph edges connecting subjects to objects via formal predicates.

answer.text: Element, Attribute, and Text Content.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Elements and attributes are components of XML hierarchical trees, not RDF graphs.

answer.text: Namespace, Textgroup, and Work Identifier.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textgroups and works are components of CTS URNs.

answer.text: XML Declaration, TEI Header, and Text Body.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are structural divisions of a TEI XML document.

name.text: 13 Question: From Strings to Things: Authority Control in TEI Markup

questiontext.text: In the context of Linked Open Data and TEI markup, what does the principle "move from strings to things" mean?

generalfeedback.text: Embedding persistent URIs in TEI `@ref` attributes transitions editions from ambiguous text strings to unambiguous, machine-resolvable entities.

answer.text: Replacing ambiguous textual names with persistent URIs in @ref attributes that resolve to unique real-world entities in global authority registers.

feedback.text: Correct. Embedding URIs links local markup to disambiguated entities in knowledge graphs, overcoming spelling variations and homonyms.

answer.text: Converting all XML text elements into binary string objects for memory optimization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The principle is ontological and semantic, not a low-level memory optimization.

answer.text: Discarding historical manuscript transcriptions in favour of modern 3D physical replicas.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The concept concerns entity disambiguation in metadata, not physical replication.

answer.text: Restricting TEI documents to numerical coordinates while banning natural language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Natural language descriptions remain, but are enriched with machine-resolvable URI handles.

name.text: 14 Question: Global Authority Registers: VIAF, Getty TGN, Getty AAT, and Wikidata

questiontext.text: Which pairing of global authority register and cataloguing domain is correct?

generalfeedback.text: Linking to centralized authority registers like VIAF, Getty TGN/AAT, Pleiades, and Wikidata ensures that entities are globally disambiguated and machine-linked.

answer.text: Getty AAT for physical materials and bookbinding terms; Pleiades for ancient Mediterranean geographic places.

feedback.text: Correct. Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus standardizes materials/techniques, while Pleiades provides georeferenced historical ancient geography.

answer.text: VIAF for leaf dimensions; Getty TGN for scribal hand classifications.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VIAF standardizes persons/organizations; TGN standardizes modern and historical geographic names.

answer.text: Pleiades for modern institutional shelfmarks; Wikidata exclusively for astronomical objects.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pleiades covers ancient geography; Wikidata is an open general knowledge graph.

answer.text: Getty AAT for author biographies; VIAF for physical parchment measurements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VIAF catalogues authors/persons; AAT catalogues art, architecture, and material concepts.

name.text: 15 Question: Mapping Manuscript Migrations (MMM): Harmonizing Heterogeneous Data

questiontext.text: How did the Mapping Manuscript Migrations (MMM) project successfully harmonize 20 million triples across SDBM, Bibale, and Oxford TEI files?

generalfeedback.text: Mapping Manuscript Migrations harmonized 20 million triples across SDBM, Bibale, and Oxford TEI files, proving that event-centric RDF models can unify heterogeneous institutional databases.

answer.text: By mapping their disparate transaction, collection, and codex structures into a shared event-centric RDF ontology based on CIDOC-CRM and FRBRoo.

feedback.text: Correct. Event-centric modeling allowed transaction observations, collections, and physical books to connect through shared provenance events.

answer.text: By forcing all three institutions to delete their existing data and re-catalogue their holdings from scratch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. MMM harmonized heterogeneous legacy data using Linked Data ontologies without destroying source databases.

answer.text: By merging all three databases into a single flat CSV spreadsheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A flat CSV cannot model complex, multi-custodial historical migration graphs.

answer.text: By restricting queries exclusively to manuscripts currently located in North America.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The project encompasses global manuscript collections across Europe and America.

name.text: 16 Question: Wikibase as a Knowledge Graph Platform for Codicology

questiontext.text: How does Wikibase structure manuscript knowledge for collaborative editing and computational queries?

generalfeedback.text: Wikibase provides an accessible, graph-native platform for hosting manuscript data, combining OpenRefine entity reconciliation with SPARQL querying capabilities.

answer.text: Using Items (Q numbers) for entities and Properties (P numbers) for predicates, with built-in SPARQL querying and OpenRefine entity reconciliation.

feedback.text: Correct. Wikibase provides an accessible, graph-native environment where codicological claims are structured as statements backed by qualifiers and references.

answer.text: By storing all data in unindexed binary PDF documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikibase is a structured semantic graph platform, not a document repository.

answer.text: By requiring all data to be hand-written in Prolog logic programming syntax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikibase uses standard MediaWiki interfaces and W3C SPARQL/RDF standards.

answer.text: By prohibiting external users from querying database statements via APIs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikibase provides open REST and SPARQL APIs for automated querying.

name.text: 17 Question: Factoid Prosopography in Syriaca.org and the SPEAR Project

questiontext.text: What distinguishes factoid prosopography (as implemented in SPEAR and Syriaca.org) from traditional historical biography?

generalfeedback.text: The SPEAR project demonstrates factoid prosopography by linking TEI event tags to RDF authority files, with every historical assertion justified by an exact CTS URN.

answer.text: It models discrete historical assertions made by specific primary texts as individual event nodes without pre-judging their absolute historical truth.

feedback.text: Correct. Factoids link claims to RDF entities and cite exact primary source locations via CTS URNs, allowing conflicting sources to be modeled transparently.

answer.text: It generates fictional historical biographies using generative AI algorithms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Factoid prosopography is a rigorous humanistic method documenting attested primary source claims.

answer.text: It records only modern historians' opinions while ignoring ancient primary witnesses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Factoids are grounded directly in primary source statements.

answer.text: It requires all historical persons to be verified by contemporary photographic evidence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ancient and medieval prosopography relies on textual and archaeological witnesses.

name.text: 18 Question: The Crisis of Brittle Citations: Why Web URLs Fail Scholarship

questiontext.text: Why are standard web URLs considered inadequate for permanent digital textual citations?

generalfeedback.text: Web URLs suffer from link rot and technology dependence; digital textual scholarship requires domain-independent, canonical citation protocols.

answer.text: They suffer from link rot, depend on specific server architectures, and fail to address abstract intellectual works at granular word/token levels.

feedback.text: Correct. URLs identify temporary web hosting locations rather than abstract intellectual texts, making citations vulnerable to obsolescence.

answer.text: Web URLs cannot be opened in modern computer browsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. URLs function well for transient browsing, but lack the permanence required for long-term scholarship.

answer.text: International copyright law prohibits scholars from publishing URLs in academic journals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. URLs are widely published, but their high rate of link decay undermines scholarly verifiability.

answer.text: URLs are limited to a maximum of ten characters, preventing detailed citation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. URLs have no such length limit; the flaw is infrastructural instability and lack of canonical semantics.

name.text: 19 Question: The CITE Architecture and the OHCO2 Text Model

questiontext.text: According to the OHCO2 text model underlying the CITE Architecture, what is a text fundamentally?

generalfeedback.text: The CITE Architecture models texts as abstract citation trees (OHCO2), using persistent URNs to identify texts and artifacts independently of physical servers.

answer.text: An ordered hierarchy of content objects—an abstract, citable tree of intellectual units (books, chapters, verses, lines) independent of physical medium.

feedback.text: Correct. OHCO2 models text as an abstract structural hierarchy rather than physical pages or digital files.

answer.text: A physical stream of ink pigments pressed onto treated animal vellum.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes a physical codex artifact, which CITE models via separate CITE2 URNs.

answer.text: A continuous, unpunctuated string of binary computer bytes stored on a server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes a physical digital file, not the abstract citable work.

answer.text: A two-dimensional grid of high-resolution digital image pixels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pixels belong to facsimile images, which are distinct from textual citation trees.

name.text: 20 Question: Anatomy of the Canonical Text Services (CTS) URN

questiontext.text: In the CTS URN urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0527.tlg001.perseus-grc1:1.1, what does the segment tlg0527 represent?

generalfeedback.text: A CTS URN decomposes text identification into a rigorous hierarchy: protocol, namespace, textgroup, work, version, exemplar, and passage.

answer.text: The textgroup identifier, representing the author or overarching textual corpus (the Septuagint Old Greek corpus).

feedback.text: Correct. CTS work identifiers follow the hierarchy: textgroup.work.version.exemplar.

answer.text: The specific physical manuscript shelfmark in the holding library.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical shelfmarks or version layers appear in the version/exemplar segment or in CITE2 URNs.

answer.text: The passage component indicating chapter and verse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 1.1 is the passage component.

answer.text: The protocol scheme identifying the communication port of the web server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. urn:cts: is the protocol scheme and greekLit is the namespace.

name.text: 21 Question: Granular Passage Addressing in CTS URNs

questiontext.text: How does a CTS URN cite an abstract work as a whole versus a specific continuous passage range within a distinct manuscript witness?

generalfeedback.text: CTS URNs support flexible granularity, enabling seamless citations from overarching works down to specific verses and continuous passage ranges.

answer.text: An abstract work omits the version and passage components, while a passage range specifies the witness version and hyphenated passage boundaries (e.g., :1.1-1.5).

feedback.text: Correct. CTS URNs provide flexible granularity, from abstract work-level citations down to specific witness passage ranges.

answer.text: Abstract works are cited using HTTP URLs, while passage ranges require SQL database queries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both levels use standardized CTS URN syntax.

answer.text: Passage ranges must be cited by physical pixel coordinates on the digital facsimile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pixel bounding boxes are handled by CITE2 image URNs, not CTS text passage ranges.

answer.text: A CTS URN cannot cite more than a single word at a time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS URNs can cite whole works, books, chapters, verses, or ranges.

name.text: 22 Question: Sub-Reference Syntax and String Indexing

questiontext.text: How does CTS sub-reference syntax disambiguate the third occurrence of the word καὶ in verse 2 of a passage?

generalfeedback.text: CTS sub-reference syntax (`@token[index]`) enables mathematical citation of specific words, repeated tokens, and character substrings within a passage.

answer.text: By appending @καὶ[3] to the passage identifier (e.g., ...:1.2@καὶ[3]).

feedback.text: Correct. Sub-reference syntax uses @token[index] to target specific words or character offsets mathematically without altering base XML markup.

answer.text: By inserting a new XML element <third_kai> into the middle of the manuscript text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sub-references address tokens externally via URNs without modifying the underlying text.

answer.text: By specifying the line number and column number in Roman numerals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS sub-references use string indexing on canonical passage nodes.

answer.text: By calculating the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the surrounding paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hashes identify Git commits, not sub-passage word occurrences in CTS.

name.text: 23 Question: CITE URNs for Non-Textual Artifacts: Folios, Images, and Papyri

questiontext.text: What is the structural role of the CITE2 URN protocol within the broader CITE Architecture?

generalfeedback.text: CITE2 URNs identify physical manuscript folios and high-resolution images, linking textual transcriptions directly to visual facsimiles.

answer.text: It provides persistent, canonical identifiers for non-textual cultural objects, physical folios, and high-resolution image regions of interest.

feedback.text: Correct. While CTS addresses textual trees, CITE2 addresses physical artifacts and image bounding boxes.

answer.text: It replaces RELAX NG as the validation engine for XML syntax checking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CITE2 is a canonical identification protocol, not a schema validation language.

answer.text: It is an encryption algorithm used to restrict access to copyrighted museum images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CITE2 is an open identification standard designed for scholarly linking and transparency.

answer.text: It converts printed books into audio speech recordings automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CITE2 identifies physical and visual objects within structured collections.

name.text: 24 Question: The Linked Fragment: Citing Lost Authors and Textual Reuses

questiontext.text: In digital classical philology, how do TEI <cit> markup and CTS URNs represent fragmentary quotations of lost authors (the "linked fragment")?

generalfeedback.text: CTS URNs and TEI `` elements model fragmentary text reuses, preserving the physical host context while linking citations to lost works.

answer.text: By anchoring the quoted text to its exact place in the surviving host manuscript while simultaneously linking its bibliographic attribution to the lost author's canonical URN.

feedback.text: Correct. This preserves the material context of the quotation without severing the fragment from its surviving host text.

answer.text: By deleting the surrounding host text so that only the lost author's words remain visible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The linked fragment methodology explicitly preserves the surrounding host text context.

answer.text: By forging synthetic complete texts using generative artificial intelligence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly digital editions document historical witnesses rather than fabricating lost texts.

answer.text: By reclassifying all fragmentary quotes as modern copyright violations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Classical textual reuse is scholarly evidence, not modern copyright infringement.

name.text: 25 Question: CTS Implementations and Web Microservices

questiontext.text: Which mandatory CTS API request verb returns the transcribed TEI XML text for a specific passage URN?

generalfeedback.text: CTS web microservices expose standardized API endpoints (`GetPassage`, `GetValidReff`) that resolve abstract URNs into structured XML text fragments.

answer.text: GetPassage

feedback.text: Correct. GetPassage resolves a passage URN and returns the corresponding structured XML text fragment.

answer.text: GetCapabilities

feedback.text: Incorrect. GetCapabilities returns an inventory of all available textgroups, works, and editions on the server.

answer.text: GetValidReff

feedback.text: Incorrect. GetValidReff returns a list of valid passage URNs within a work or range.

answer.text: DropDatabase

feedback.text: Incorrect. DropDatabase is a destructive SQL database command, not a CTS request verb.

name.text: 26 Question: Integrating CTS URNs into the teiHeader and Body

questiontext.text: How does a TEI document structurally align its transcribed body text with the Canonical Text Services hierarchy?

generalfeedback.text:
Embedding CTS URNs in `` and structural `

` elements aligns the TEI XML tree with the canonical citation hierarchy.

answer.text: By nesting <div type="textpart" subtype="chapter" n="1"> elements whose hierarchy mirrors the canonical citation tree.

feedback.text: Correct. Structural <div type="textpart"> elements with @n numbers enable automated CTS parsers to harvest citable text nodes.

answer.text: By formatting all text as a single unbroken string inside <teiHeader>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transcriptions belong in <text><body>, not the metadata header, and require hierarchical division.

answer.text: By removing all XML tags and uploading a raw Microsoft Word document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS integration requires structured, valid TEI XML divisions.

answer.text: By replacing ancient verse numbers with modern page numbers from a 19th-century print edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS relies on canonical intellectual divisions, not transient print page numbers.

name.text: 27 Question: Hands-On: Validating and Enriching the Primary Witness Header

questiontext.text: What are the core technical tasks required to transition a hand-written TEI header into a validated, linked-data-enriched record in Lesson 2.2?

generalfeedback.text: The validation lab transforms raw manual markup into a certified, schema-valid, linked-data-enriched digital manuscript record.

answer.text: Resolving schema nesting errors in VS Code, converting dates to ISO 8601, verifying @hand Schematron pointers, and embedding VIAF/AAT URIs and CTS URNs.

feedback.text: Correct. These systematic steps ensure both internal structural validity and external semantic interoperability.

answer.text: Deleting the manuscript description and replacing it with an automated Wikipedia summary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The lab enriches the primary codicological ground truth rather than replacing it with secondary summaries.

answer.text: Converting the XML file into an uncompressed WAV audio file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text encoding and linked data remain in XML and RDF text formats.

answer.text: Removing all attribute quotes to test whether the parser can operate in non-strict mode.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unquoted attributes violate basic well-formedness and cause immediate fatal parser crashes.

name.text: 28 Question: Extracting RDF Triples from TEI via XSLT and SPARQL

questiontext.text: How are validated TEI manuscript headers converted into queryable Linked Open Data triples for ingestion into triple stores?

generalfeedback.text: Validated TEI headers are transformed into RDF triples via XSLT, enabling lightning-fast SPARQL queries across decentralized international repositories.

answer.text: An XSLT stylesheet parses the XML tree, transforming elements like <msDesc> and <persName> into RDF/XML or Turtle triples queryable via SPARQL.

feedback.text: Correct. XSLT automates the extraction of graph triples from hierarchical XML trees.

answer.text: By printing out the XML file and scanning it with an optical bar code reader.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Triple extraction is an automated software transformation via XSLT scripts.

answer.text: By manually typing 20 million lines of SQL insert commands in a terminal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XSLT stylesheets automate batch graph extraction across thousands of files.

answer.text: By deleting all element tags and preserving only numerical dates.

name.text: 29 Question: Auditing the Deterministic Pass: Clean Validation as the Stage Gate

questiontext.text: Why does the RELS 398 curriculum enforce a strict zero-error validation stage gate before allowing students to proceed to AI benchmarking?

generalfeedback.text: A zero-error validation report is the mandatory stage gate that certifies your ground truth before comparative AI benchmarking.

answer.text: An unvalidated or broken XML baseline cannot serve as a scientific ground truth, corrupting all downstream comparative measurements and error scoring.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Triple Infrastructure of Digital Philology

questiontext.text: How do TEI XML, RDF Linked Open Data, and CTS URNs combine to form the foundational infrastructure of modern digital textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: TEI XML, RDF Linked Open Data, and CTS URNs form the three-part computational infrastructure that makes digital textual scholarship permanent, interoperable, and reproducible.

answer.text: TEI provides granular internal codicological markup; RDF connects entities to global knowledge graphs; CTS provides permanent, technology-independent canonical citations.

feedback.text: Correct. Together, these three layers guarantee internal structural fidelity, external semantic interoperability, and permanent citable addressing.

answer.text: TEI manages web hosting servers; RDF designs user interface layouts; CTS prints paper volumes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. None of these standards perform server hosting, graphic UI layout, or physical printing.

answer.text: They serve as three competing commercial products that cannot be used in the same project.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are open, complementary standards that integrate seamlessly in digital editions.

answer.text: They replace the need for historical scholarship by automating textual criticism completely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They provide computational infrastructure for human scholarship rather than replacing critical judgement.
